items.title: Tom Brown Interview, 1956
items.q: I've made over 100 recordings with Johnny Wiggs that I think are very good.

ctx.x: Well, Art, they all say that I was the one that took the first Dixieland band to Chicago.

So it must be so. This band was later turned into jazz by Chicago local musicians. Well, we had the finest kind of tempo and rhythm that took the world by surprise and started something really big. That it is all over the world today. I've enjoyed the fruits of jazz since 1950. I made a lot of photograph records which have made hits. I've made some good records with Yerkes. Yerkes, Dance Orchestra. Yerkes, Happy Six. Yerkes, Southern Five. Yerkes, Jazz Marimba Orchestra. Ray Miller's Black and White Melody Boys.…

items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine, Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine and Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1959-02-27
items.q: I had Tom and Teddoh playing with me.

ctx.x: I wanted to ask you, did Tom Brown play with you? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He's one of the two Teddors. I had Tom and Teddoh playing with me. Yeah. I had five bands Johnny going all the time. Steve Brown played with you too, huh? That's Ted. That's his name. Who? Ted, huh? Ted. Ted. They called him Steve later on. Yeah. Teddoh. Yeah. Teddoh. Uh-huh. Yeah. They called him Steve. Yeah. He was in town recently too. Yeah, I know. I met him. He looked me up. Yeah. He's a wonderful bass player.
There's Merritt. He's good bass player. He's right here. Merritt.

items.title: Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1969-12-14
items.q: I heard Tom Brown's name mentioned, and I recall when I was a boy, and that goes back in the 20s, he operated a music supply store on a magazine near Jackson Avenue. He and his wife, do you recall that? Yeah, I remember.

ctx.x: slam the door in nurses' faces. It was done out at the hospital, the TB hospital out the lake. I had to slam the door in audits' faces. I had to take phones off of hooks and brush off the hair which is caused by these platter machines. And lo and behold, if we didn't get 12 of fairly good sides, which are on the market now. Okay, and we're going to be hearing some of those, but first we have to bring you this message. Hi, Karate, after Shaven. Cologne presents. All right, we want to wish a very happy birthday…

baby. That will be coming up shortly, but we want to go back to the multi-phones with another call here for you. Good morning. You're on the air with Dick Allen of Tulane University. And Mr. Johnny Wiggs. Yes, sir. Go ahead. This is Eddie Jazz. One of the original jazz man. See, I like to set the record straight about jazz. Jazz is only 55 years old. There's no such thing as jazz before that. And that was just what's going on now. Everybody is using one another's questions about jazz. Now, I'm related to Tom…

Johnny said that nobody hurt him. I can't think of his name right now. But he played against Louis Armstrong on a boat, and Louis Armstrong put his horn down, said that he could pass Emmett Hardy that I'm talking about.

I just wasn't exposed to the right people. They had them. Tom Brown was playing at that time and Tom Brown could always play well. But I just didn't hear them. The cornet players that I heard around town, I won't mention any names, but they played in the style which we called corny. To this day, people are still playing like that on the west coast. A lot of people are raving about those bands on the west coast. To me, it's still imitation jazz. It's corny. Well, they had many white cornet players that I heard…
Emmett Hardy, no. Some people you know rave about how... I have heard nothing but good about him.
